organization: U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (implemented by Legacy International)
opportunity_type: government-funded exchange with mentorship/STEM-career-exploration component (hybrid, not a classic single-employer internship)
location: Virginia Tech University; one of Austin/Cincinnati/Denver/Detroit/Kansas City/Seattle; Washington DC
citizenship_requirement: Verbatim (techgirlsglobal.org eligibility page): 'Eligible candidates must be citizens and current residents of 2026 participating countries.'
residency_requirement: Same clause as citizenship_requirement -- citizenship AND current residency in an eligible country are both required.
work_authorization_required: false -- participants travel on a J-1 exchange visitor visa arranged by the program, not as employees; official page notes dual citizens living abroad are NOT eligible to travel on the program or get a J-1 visa.
international_eligibility: Yes -- the program is structurally an international exchange for applicants from 37 eligible countries/territories outside the US, plus US peers.
turkiye_accessible: yes -- Turkiye is explicitly named on the official 2026 eligible-country list under 'Europe & Eurasia'.
age_requirement: 15-17 years old at program start; verbatim birth-date window 'July 12, 2008 and July 11, 2011' for the July 11, 2026 start.
grade_requirement: not specified by grade level; eligibility is age-based only. IMPORTANT: program is for girls/young women only -- this sex restriction is a decision-critical eligibility fact not captured by any other schema field.
application_open: unknown exact 2026 open date; historically opens several months before the January deadline
application_deadline: 2026 cycle: closed as of this research (deadline was January 20, 2026, per aggregator reporting of the official cycle; decisions communicated by mid-April 2026). Next (2027) cycle deadline not yet published.
program_dates: 23-day in-person exchange beginning July 11, 2026, followed by approximately 7 months of mentorship (including pre- and post-exchange).
cost_verbatim: Official page lists covered expenses: 'Visa Fee', 'Round trip international airfare from participant home country to the United States', 'Housing during program... Double occupancy dormitory accommodations', 'Meals during program - Breakfast, lunch, and dinner', 'Local transportation to group program events', 'Cultural events organized by Legacy International', and 'Emergency health insurance'.
financial_aid: N/A -- fully funded by the U.S. Department of State; no separate aid application needed.
prize_or_stipend: None beyond the fully-funded program costs -- this is not a wage/stipend program.
selection_process: Competitive written application via the official eligibility-and-application page; selects roughly 111 participants annually across all 37 eligible countries plus US peers (2026 cohort).
selectivity_evidence: unknown -- no official acceptance-rate percentage found. Only cohort size (111 across 37 countries/territories for 2026) is published; applicant-pool size is not, so no rate can be computed without guessing.
required_documents: unknown -- application-form contents were not fetched this session beyond the eligibility page.
notes: STRUCTURAL NOTE: this is a government-funded mentorship / tech-exchange / STEM-career-exploration program, not a classic 'work at one company' internship -- no single host employer, no job description, no wages. Recorded because it matches the brief's 'structured shadowing/mentorship-internship hybrid' category and is one of the very few programs found in this entire research pass that is BOTH genuinely competitively selected AND explicitly, officially open to a Turkish 14-18-year-old (girls only). Not a pay-to-play broker -- fully government funded. This is the single strongest find of this research pass for ORYN's stated Turkiye/international audience.

turkiye_accessible: yes -- free, online, no application or nationality restriction found; reachable by a Turkish student with an internet connection.
age_requirement: unknown / inconsistent -- no explicit minimum age stated on the pages directly fetched. Secondary sources (university career centers) describe it as suitable for 'high school students (16+)' while other secondary sources claim no age restriction at all. Recorded as unresolved rather than guessed.
grade_requirement: none -- open to any student status per the platform's own positioning
application_open: N/A -- no application process; free self-service account creation
program_dates: N/A -- self-paced; individual modules typically take a few hours
cost_verbatim: Direct fetch of theforage.com/about: 'Forage is always free for students, self-paced & open-access.' Revenue model is stated as charging employers to host programs, not charging students.

selectivity_evidence: not applicable -- open enrollment, not a selective program

Forage's own verbatim language on international-student/no-work-authorization eligibility could NOT be directly captured this session (fetch attempts to their FAQ returned question headings without answer text, and a follow-up fetch attempt to the FAQ URL failed outright) -- that specific claim rests on consistent third-party paraphrase rather than my own direct-source capture.

It is genuinely valuable as a free, globally accessible career-exploration resource, and it genuinely reaches Turkish students with zero cost or barrier -- which is exactly why it is recorded here -- but ORYN must never present it to a student as equivalent to a competitively-selected internship such as OEC-001 or OEC-003.

organization: EY Foundation (the charitable arm of EY UK)

work_authorization_required: true, in effect -- this is paid UK work experience, so UK right-to-work would apply to any participant; the official pages did not use the literal phrase 'work authorization' because the state-school-plus-means-tested-benefit eligibility gate already presumes a UK-resident applicant.
international_eligibility: No mechanism found for a non-UK-resident applicant -- every stated criterion (state-school attendance, UK means-tested benefits) presumes UK residency.
turkiye_accessible: no -- requires current attendance at a UK state school plus UK means-tested benefit eligibility (free school meals / Education Maintenance Allowance / college bursary); structurally inaccessible to a student based in Turkey.

application_open: unknown exact date for the 2026/27 cycle -- not captured this session
application_deadline: unknown for the 2026/27 cycle -- not captured this session

cost_verbatim: Work experience is explicitly described as paid (participants are paid, not charged); exact wage rate not stated on the page fetched.

prize_or_stipend: Paid work experience; exact rate not disclosed on the page fetched.
selection_process: Application-based; must satisfy the income/benefit eligibility gate plus stated academic thresholds. Described as competitive but no numeric acceptance rate found.
selectivity_evidence: unknown -- no official acceptance-rate figure found on the pages reviewed.
verification_status: VERIFIED_CURRENT for eligibility structure (age, year group, state-school-plus-means-tested-benefit gate, academic thresholds) via direct fetch of the official eyfoundation.com page. NOT verified this session: current-cycle application deadline, exact wage rate, and total places available.
notes: Strong example of a genuinely merit-and-need-based (not open-enrollment, not pay-to-play) UK work-experience programme with real selection criteria -- but its eligibility design (UK state school plus UK means-tested benefits) makes it a clean, honest illustration of a structural access barrier for ORYN's international/Turkish user base, rather than a gap in this research.

organization: Cristo Rey Network (a network of approximately 40 Catholic high schools, each running its own CWSP office)
opportunity_type: integrated paid work-study -- real corporate jobs, one day per week for all 4 years of high school, built into school enrollment
subject_area: general professional work experience (office/administrative roles across many industries, dependent on each school's local corporate partners)
subcategory: paid real jobs at host companies, performed in 4-person student job-share teams that together fill one full-time position
delivery_mode: in-person, remote, or hybrid depending on the host company's arrangement
location: approximately 40 school sites across roughly 24 U.S. states
citizenship_requirement: Per search-engine synthesis of the official cristoreynetwork.org employer-facing page: 'Students must be eligible to work in the United States.' NOTE: I was not able to independently re-confirm this exact sentence via my own direct WebFetch of that page this session -- see verification note.
residency_requirement: Must be enrolled as a student at one of the approximately 40 Cristo Rey Network schools -- this is not an open application program; enrollment at a specific partner school is the actual gating mechanism, not a separate work-study application.
work_authorization_required: true. An official Cristo Rey school FAQ (Don Bosco Cristo Rey, dbcr.org) states the programme operates under a 'special provision from the U.S. Department of Labor' allowing employment from age 14 -- US-labor-law-specific machinery not available to a student without US work eligibility.
international_eligibility: No -- the model requires physical enrollment at one of ~40 US Catholic high schools; there is no direct-application pathway for a student not already enrolled at one of these schools.
turkiye_accessible: no -- requires enrollment at one of ~40 specific US Catholic high schools plus US work eligibility; not accessible to a student based in Turkey.
age_requirement: Verbatim (Don Bosco Cristo Rey FAQ, dbcr.org): 'Students must be at least 14 years old to participate in the Corporate Work Study Program.'
grade_requirement: All 4 years of high school (grades 9-12) -- work-study is a mandatory, integrated part of enrollment at a Cristo Rey school, not an elective add-on. Verbatim (dbcr.org FAQ): 'Yes, all students are required to participate in the Corporate Work Study Program (CWSP).'
application_open: N/A -- gated by admission to a specific school, not a separate work-study application
application_deadline: N/A -- tied to each school's own admissions cycle
program_dates: One full day per week during the school year, all 4 years of high school
cost: N/A to apply to CWSP itself -- tied to each school's tuition, which the earned wages directly offset
cost_verbatim: Verbatim (dbcr.org FAQ): employer fees are 'applied directly and proportionately to each student's tuition costs' rather than paid to students as take-home wages during the school year. Cristo Rey Network's own framing: students 'earn a significant portion of their own private education costs.'
financial_aid: The entire model functions as a tuition-offset mechanism for a student population that could not otherwise afford private-school tuition -- need-based by design.
prize_or_stipend: Wages are paid by the host employer to the CWSP office and credited against tuition, not typically disbursed as a take-home stipend.
selection_process: No competitive selection for the work-study placement itself once admitted to the school. Verbatim (cristoreynetwork.org): 'The Corporate Work Study office works directly with the employer to generate a job description and a partnership experience,' then places a pre-formed 4-student team with the host company.
selectivity_evidence: not applicable -- mandatory participation for all enrolled students, not a competitive program.
required_documents: unknown -- tied to each individual school's own admissions process, not researched this session
official_application_url: N/A -- apply to a specific Cristo Rey Network school (see cristoreynetwork.org/schools), not to CWSP directly
verification_status: PARTIALLY_VERIFIED -- program mechanism, mandatory participation, tuition-offset structure, and the 14-year-old minimum (at one specific network school, Don Bosco Cristo Rey) confirmed via direct fetch of official cristoreynetwork.org and dbcr.org pages. NOT independently re-confirmed via my own direct fetch: the exact 'eligible to work in the United States' phrase (came from search-engine synthesis of the official employer page, not my own verbatim capture on a repeat fetch) and the current total school count (my direct fetch of cristoreynetwork.org/about-us returned HTTP 404; the ~40-school count rests on Wikipedia's citation of the network's own figures, and the Wikipedia page itself shows an internal inconsistency, citing both 38 and 40 schools).
notes: Textbook example of the research brief's 'school-gated' structural-barrier pattern: this is a completely real, serious, merit-based-by-admission work experience (NOT a pay-to-play broker -- real employers define real job descriptions and Cristo Rey places genuine working teams), but access runs entirely through admission to one specific US high school network, not through an open application any ORYN user could complete. Also a clean, explicit case of a de facto work-authorization barrier for this category, exactly as the research brief anticipated.

canonical_name: Absolute Internship -- High School Internship Program
opportunity_type: COMMERCIAL PAY-TO-PLACE INTERNSHIP BROKER -- explicitly NOT a merit-selected internship (see notes)
subject_area: Business, Creative, Tech, or Non-Profit -- student selects a career track
delivery_mode: in-person (11-14 international city locations) or remote
location: Bangkok, Barcelona, Copenhagen, Hong Kong, Lisbon, London, Madrid, Paris, Seoul, Shanghai, Singapore, Stockholm, Taipei, Tokyo per the official page, plus a separate remote track

work_authorization_required: false / not applicable -- the company's own marketing sells this as a guaranteed placement/experience product rather than formal employment, sidestepping the work-authorization question this category otherwise raises.
international_eligibility: Yes -- explicitly designed for international students/families, since the entire business model is placing students in a foreign city.
turkiye_accessible: yes -- no nationality restriction found; accessible to any family in Turkey able to pay the program fee. See notes on cost/selectivity caveat before treating this as equivalent to a merit-based opportunity.

grade_requirement: high school students generally; no specific grade floor found

selectivity_evidence: N/A -- explicitly guaranteed, not selective. No acceptance rate exists because there is no merit-based rejection path once enrollment/payment is complete.
required_documents: unknown -- likely a payment/enrollment form only, consistent with the 'guaranteed' framing; not independently confirmed
official_application_url: https://absoluteinternship.com/dates-fees/ (the high-school-specific dates-fees path returned HTTP 404 on direct fetch this session; the general dates-fees page was reachable)
verification_status: VERIFIED that this is a fee-based guaranteed-placement commercial product (not a merit-selected internship) via direct fetch of the official absoluteinternship.com pages. NOT fully verified: the exact undiscounted price specifically for the high-school track (direct fetch captured only promotional-discount banner text, not a clean base price; the EUR 3,595-11,895 range comes from the company's general dates-fees page and is not confirmed to be the exact figure applied to the high-school-specific track).
notes: EXPLICIT PAY-TO-PLAY FLAG, per the research brief's specific instruction: this is a commercial placement-brokerage business whose core product is a family-paid GUARANTEED internship, not a competitively-selected opportunity -- the host organization does not select the student on merit; the company sells access to a placement. This must never be presented to an ORYN user as equivalent in kind to a genuinely selective internship such as OEC-001 (TechGirls) or OEC-003 (EY Smart Futures). Recorded specifically because the research brief asked for an explicit, clearly-labeled example of this business model, which is extremely common in the 'international internship for teens' search space (near-identical competitors include Intern Abroad HQ and Global Experiences; CRCC Asia was also checked and excluded because its own site states an 18+ minimum, so it does not even superficially reach this age group). ORYN's opportunity engine should give this whole category a structurally different UI/labeling treatment, never listing it as a peer of merit-based programs.

organization: Ladder Internships (commercial internship-placement company founded by Harvard alumni)
subcategory: 8-week virtual project-based placement with a partner startup, sold in priced tiers (Start-up / CEO / Combination)
country: company operates internationally; host startups vary
work_authorization_required: false -- this is remote/virtual project work performed by a fee-paying participant, not formal paid employment, so conventional work-authorization rules do not apply in the way they would for an in-person paid role.
international_eligibility: Yes -- remote/virtual by design and marketed as open to students worldwide.
turkiye_accessible: yes -- fully remote and fee-based rather than nationality-gated; accessible to a paying family in Turkey with internet access.
age_requirement: unknown exact floor -- marketed at 'ambitious students,' commonly described by secondary sources as reaching high-school and college age, but no explicit numeric floor was confirmed from the official site this session.
application_open: rolling -- multiple 8-week cohorts run per year
cost: USD 2,990 (Start-up Internship) / USD 4,990 (CEO Internship) / USD 7,400 (Combination Programme), per secondary reporting
cost_verbatim: Per secondary reporting of Ladder's own published pricing (Immerse Education, Young Founders Lab, CollegeVine all describe matching figures): 'The Start-up Internship costs USD $2,990, the CEO Internship costs $4,990... the Combination Programme costs $7,400.' NOT independently re-confirmed via my own direct fetch of a Ladder pricing page this session -- see verification note.
financial_aid: Ladder states it offers need-based financial aid/scholarships, but per secondary reporting 'only 10-20% of interns receive financial support.'
prize_or_stipend: none -- the fee is paid by the family/student; this is not a stipend paid to the student.
selection_process: Application plus interview; the company then matches the student to a 'best fit' project at a partner startup based on interests and interview notes, and the student has final say on whether to proceed. This is a real matching step, but it occurs only within the pool of students who have already paid or been granted aid -- it is not a competition for a scarce free/unpaid slot.
selectivity_evidence: unknown -- no official acceptance-rate published; the financial-aid rate (10-20% of interns) is not the same thing as an overall admission rate.
required_documents: unknown -- application plus interview, per above
verification_status: PARTIALLY_VERIFIED -- program structure (8 weeks, remote, startup placement, tiered fee model) is well-corroborated across multiple independent secondary sources describing the same official ladderinternships.com pricing and structure consistently, but I was not able to successfully WebFetch Ladder's own pricing page directly this session to capture the exact verbatim price line myself -- treat the exact dollar figures as secondary-corroborated, not self-verified from the primary source.
notes: Second explicit pay-to-play example, deliberately a different flavor from OEC-006: this one is virtual/remote and startup-focused (vs. Absolute Internship's in-person/global-city model), showing the business model spans multiple product shapes. Real startups are involved and a real (if thin) matching step exists, making this a slightly softer case than Absolute Internship's fully 'guaranteed' framing -- but it remains fundamentally a family-paid product with only a 10-20% aid rate, not a free merit-selected opportunity, and should be labeled accordingly to students.
